title: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Turbulent randomness is intrinsically generated at the level of large-scale fluid motion

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The randomness seen in turbulent fluids is mostly neither inserted from outside nor inherited from molecular randomness, but is intrinsically generated by the dynamics of the large-scale fluid motion itself.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Instead, what seems to be happening is that intrinsic randomness generation occurs directly at the level of large-scale fluid motion.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 8, “Implications for Everyday Systems”; section “Fluid Flow” (from p. 376), p. 382. Scope: turbulent fluid flow

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch08-08: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing turbulence simulations permit counterfactual perturbations and scale-resolved energy analyses. They cover canonical flows and can test whether large-scale dynamics sustain randomness. Causal attribution among forcing noise, initial uncertainty, and intrinsic instability remains confounded in observational records.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare turbulence statistics in repeated flows with controlled macroscopic forcing while varying external disturbances and molecular noise in matched simulations. The claim is supported if large-scale dynamics generate nearly invariant turbulent statistics after those inputs are suppressed or varied, but refuted if output randomness tracks them.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Chaotic amplification makes internally generated and unmeasured input randomness observationally similar.

Most existing datasets do not independently vary molecular noise.

Mostly needs a variance attribution convention.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Deterministic simulations already produce turbulence, which bears directly on the claim that molecular noise is not required. Separating that intrinsic cascade from disturbances that entered through the boundaries is much harder in experiments, and public databases are single realizations of a few geometries. The claim is testable for those flows and not as a statement about turbulent fluids in general.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare deterministic Navier-Stokes simulations that contain no molecular noise with the same flows under added microscopic noise or altered inflow perturbations, and attribute the turbulent variance by scale. Turbulence that persists without molecular noise and without external forcing fluctuations would support intrinsic large-scale generation; turbulence that disappears when those sources are removed would count against it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Laboratory inflows and boundaries always inject disturbances, so an external contribution is hard to set to zero.

Mostly is a partition of variance that different decompositions assign differently.
